supported.seed-decision-document:
## Summary

Falcon-3 flies with **two flight controllers** in an active/standby arrangement. The standby board takes over
automatically when the active board stops sending a heartbeat.

## Failover sequence

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Active controller] -->|heartbeat| W[Watchdog]
    W -->|heartbeat missed twice| S[Standby controller]
    S --> T[Takes over the actuator bus]
    T --> L[Logs the event for the post-flight review]
```

## Options compared

| Option | Mass added | Unit cost | In-flight recovery |
|---|---|---|---|
| Single controller, cold spare | 0 g | Lowest | None |
| Dual, automatic failover | 45 g | Moderate | Yes |
| Triple modular redundancy | 110 g | Highest | Yes, with voting |

## Open questions

- Handover time must stay below the **200 ms** the autopilot tolerates.
- The standby board needs its own power rail.
supported.seeded: Use a single flight controller /: Falcon-3 will ship with one primary flight controller board and a cold-spare swapped in by ground crew between flights, rather than dual-redundant boards flying together.
Early Falcon-3 prototypes carried a single flight controller with no in-flight redundancy.
(1) Single controller, cold-spare swapped between flights. (2) Dual-redundant controllers flying together with in-flight failover.
Option 1 — single controller with a cold-spare.

Dual-redundant hardware wasn't available within the initial flight-test budget or schedule; a cold-spare gets most of the reliability benefit for ground-based utility inspection flights, where an in-flight failure can safely abort to a landing.
Loses in-flight recovery from a controller failure; acceptable for the initial operating envelope but revisit once flights move over populated areas.
supported.seeded: Adopt dual-redundant flight co /: Falcon-3 will fly with two flight controller boards in an active/standby arrangement, with automatic in-flight failover, superseding the earlier single-controller design.
Planned operations now include inspection routes over populated infrastructure corridors, where a single controller failure could mean an uncontrolled descent rather than a safe abort.
(1) Keep the single-controller/cold-spare design. (2) Dual-redundant controllers with automatic failover. (3) Triple modular redundancy.
Matches the reliability bar for flight over populated areas without the cost/weight penalty of full triple modular redundancy, which the airframe's payload budget can't absorb.
Adds airframe weight and BOM cost per unit; avionics firmware needs an active/standby handover path that didn't exist before (tracked as its own firmware requirement).
supported.seeded: Migrate firmware OTA update ch /: Not yet decided — evaluating whether to require cryptographically signed firmware images for over-the-air updates before the next fleet-wide rollout.
Current OTA channel accepts unsigned images verified only by a checksum, adequate for an internal test fleet but not for a customer-operated one.
supported.seeded: Select the cellular modem vend /: Falcon-3 will standardise on one cellular modem vendor for its telemetry uplink.
Two vendors are qualified; field trials finished last month.
supported.seeded: Adopt a 3-axis gimbal as the s /: Falcon-3 inspection payloads will mount on a 3-axis gimbal.
supported.seeded: Fuse IMU and GPS with a dual-r /: Avionics will run two independent sensor-fusion estimators and vote on their output.
Sub-project-level consequence of the Falcon-3 dual-redundancy decision.
